newsitem.title: Russia: Russia still tough on NATO ahead of Albright visit.
newsitem.headline: Russia still tough on NATO ahead of Albright visit.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright flies to Moscow on Thursday with a package of measures aimed at overcoming Russian objections to NATO expansion, but the Kremlin made clear she faced a tough task wooing her hosts.
Albright, who has been touring European capitals in a bid to forge a united Western front before her tricky negotiations with Russia, was due to arrive in Moscow at 3 p.m. (1200 GMT).
NATO's plans to admit former Warsaw Pact countries will dominate her two days of talks with Russian officials that culminate in a meeting on Friday with President Boris Yeltsin.

Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency on Thursday that Russia remained implacably opposed to NATO expansion, which it regards as a direct threat to its own security.
"(Our opposition) will remain, whatever the outcome of the negotiations between Russia and the Atlantic alliance," Interfax quoted him as saying.

In a front-page article in the liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily, Boris Berezovsky, deputy secretary of Russia's policy-making Security Council, said NATO's plan was as dangerous for the West as for Russia because it redivided Europe into two camps.

"It is above all a decision by the West that Russia cannot be integrated...It is a totally aggressive decision with regard to Russia that is also exceptionally dangerous for the West itself," said Berezovsky, also an influential businessman.
Yastrzhembsky repeated the Kremlin's demand for a legally binding contract providing security guarantees for Russia in the event of NATO's expansion.
"The signing of a legally binding document between Russia and NATO is meant to reduce to a minimum the unavoidable negative consequences of the bloc's expansion," he said.

"The conclusion of such a document would be not a gift to Russia but a demonstration of healthy pragmatism by the Western countries, based on their understanding of their own interests of national security," Yastrzhembsky added.

NATO wants closer ties with Russia, which it recognises as an indispensable part of any future European security arrangement, but is reluctant to sign any document that would give Moscow an effective veto over its decision-making.
During her visit Albright is expected to outline several major new initiatives, including the offer of a joint NATO-Russia military brigade, mainly to be used in peacekeeping.
Albright is also expected to explain sweeping changes to a landmark arms control treaty agreed by NATO allies on Wednesday in another bid to win Moscow round.

The changes to the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty take account of several Russian objections to existing ceilings on arsenals, which Moscow says are rooted in the Cold War and put it at a disadvantage.
Despite these moves, Albright will find a deeply sceptical mood in Moscow, where many suspect her eastern European background has coloured her approach to Russia, something she firmly denies.
The tough-talking, Czech-born diplomat is depicted in the Russian press as an "iron lady" in the mould of hawkish former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.
"The aphorism "a diplomat's tongue is meant to hide his thoughts" is completely foreign to Madeleine Albright," said the popular daily Moskovsky Komsomolets on Thursday.
The foreign ministers of Germany and Italy have also visited Moscow this week in a bid to sell NATO's plans but have found a rare consensus among Russians across the political spectrum.
"Everyone I have met has shown resistance to NATO enlargement," said Germany's Klaus Kinkel on Wednesday.
